analysis.one_liner: Phases nicotine in cigarettes down to near-zero over six years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote after being referred to a House subcommittee in June 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have treated nicotine like the addictive drug the Surgeon General says it is. It would make it illegal to sell cigarettes with more than 10 mg of nicotine starting in 1997, then cut that ceiling every year — 8 mg, 6 mg, 4 mg, 2 mg — until 2002, when cigarettes could contain only 0.05 mg, essentially none. Enforcement would run through the same Food and Drug Administration rules used for other adulterated products. The bill never moved past its first referral to a subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, it would have mainly helped children who experiment with smoking and current smokers who want to quit. The bill's own findings cite the Surgeon General's conclusion that nicotine rapidly addict up to half of children who try tobacco, and that most adult smokers started before age 20. Removing nicotine would remove the hook that turns a first cigarette into a decades-long habit, and it would have cut into a product the findings say kills more than 419,000 Americans a year and costs the health system about $50 billion annually.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and smokers who want to quit

how_it_helps.text: Sets annual limits on nicotine per cigarette starting at 10 mg in 1997 and dropping to 0.05 mg by 2002, effectively ending addictive cigarettes.
Covers all tobacco products: the Secretary must set comparable nicotine reductions for cigars, pipe tobacco, and smokeless tobacco, not just cigarettes.
Enforces the limits through existing Food and Drug Administration interstate-commerce provisions, so selling an over-limit product would be a federal violation.
The bill's findings state that manufacturers already have the technology to remove all or virtually all nicotine from tobacco products, so the industry could comply without new invention.

analysis.who_pays: Cigarette manufacturers would bear the cost of reengineering their products and would lose the addictive loyalty that keeps customers smoking. Tobacco growers and the leaf-processing industry would face falling demand for normal tobacco. Addicted smokers who had no intention of quitting would lose the product they rely on, and some public-health analysts worry a black market in full-nicotine cigarettes could develop once the limits bite.

drawbacks.text: The six-year phase-down to 0.05 mg is the most aggressive part: long-term smokers who don't want to quit would face withdrawal or be pushed toward an illegal market, since the bill makes any over-limit cigarette contraband rather than merely regulating how it's marketed.

The bill rests on FDA authority under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, an approach the tobacco industry fought in court throughout the 1990s; the legal footing was contested at the time and the FDA's authority over tobacco was not settled until later litigation.

Low-nicotine cigarettes do not automatically mean less smoking: some smokers compensate by smoking more cigarettes or inhaling more deeply to get the nicotine their bodies are used to, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it worked as intended, the benefit would be enormous — the bill's findings attribute more than 419,000 deaths a year and about $50 billion in annual health spending to smoking, and nicotine is the piece that keeps new smokers coming back. The main honest objections are practical: addicted smokers who don't want to quit would bear real costs, compensation behavior and black markets could blunt the gains, and the whole scheme depended on FDA legal authority the industry was challenging. Even so, this was one of the most direct legislative attacks ever proposed on the mechanism that causes smoking addiction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee, sent to its health subcommittee a few days later, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Meehan, a Massachusetts Democrat, introduced the bill on June 15, 1995, joined by Rep. Hansen, a Utah Republican.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced.

Four days later, on June 19, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment — and the record shows no hearing, markup, vote, or further action of any kind for the rest of the 104th Congress.
It drew 10 cosponsors, 8 Democrats and 2 Republicans, far short of the support needed to compel committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cigarette manufacturers and the tobacco industry came out ahead: the bill that would have forced nicotine out of their products never advanced past a subcommittee referral, and no vote was ever taken. Smokers trying to quit and children who would have been spared addiction got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan but tiny — a Democratic sponsor with 8 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors — and its death came not from a vote but from committee inaction under a Republican-chared committee.

industries.note: The bill would force them to strip nicotine from their products and would make addictive cigarettes contraband, attacking the feature that keeps customers smoking for life. The bill's findings quote a senior industry research scientist describing the cigarette as a 'dispenser for a dose unit of nicotine.'

Near-zero-nicotine cigarettes would cut demand for conventional tobacco leaf, hurting farm income in tobacco-growing states. The bill covers cigars, pipe tobacco, and smokeless products too, so the hit would spread across the crop.

Retailers would lose sales as addicted customers quit or switch, though they would still sell the de-nicotined products during the phase-down. Enforcement falls on interstate commerce, so sellers of over-limit product would face federal penalties.
